item.title: Ex-SJSU volleyball coach files new lawsuit alleging retaliation for Trump support, religion amid trans scandal
item.description: Melissa Batie-Smoose's new federal lawsuit alleges Todd Kress mocked her Trump support and religious beliefs before SJSU stripped her duties.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: Former San Jose State University volleyball assistant coach has filed a new lawsuit over her alleged treatment during and before the school's scandal involving transgender athlete Blaire Fleming and female teammate Brooke Slusser. Melissa Batie-Smoose filed an initial lawsuit last October, but it was dismissed in September.

But she's not backing down, and is now making new allegations about what happened before she was suspended and eventually let go from her position.

Her new complaint alleges that SJSU head volleyball coach Todd Kress mocked her for supporting Donald Trump in front of players, reacted with hostility to her religious objections to a transgender athlete’s participation, and made her feel "physically unsafe" during certain interactions.

The complaint alleges she repeatedly told Kress, "in substance," that "God made man and woman" and that her beliefs prevented her from treating a male athlete as female. She claims Kress responded with hostility toward those beliefs and disparaged her politics.

CAMPUS CONFLICT EXPOSED AT THE CORE OF SJSU'S MESSY FIGHT VS TRUMP ADMIN OVER VOLLEYBALL SCANDAL

"Kress would also berate her during practice in front of the athletes, calling her ‘Trump-loving’ or a ‘Trump lover’ and mocking her political affiliation," the complaint states.

Elsewhere, the filing alleges that Kress knew she was a Republican who had voted for Trump and used those remarks to damage her relationship with players, excluded her from meetings and reduced coaching duties.

The relationship at the center of the new complaint began well before the controversy.

Batie-Smoose says she worked with Kress at Florida State in 2006 and again at Fairfield University from 2019 through 2022. When Kress moved to San Jose State, she accepted the associate head coaching position and relocated her family from Connecticut to California in January 2023.

Batie-Smoose has previously alleged she learned that Fleming was transgender only after arriving in 2023.

Over the next two seasons, Batie-Smoose says, disagreements about Fleming’s participation became entangled with her relationship with Kress, her responsibilities on the court and her standing inside the athletic department.

One alleged confrontation described in the complaint began with a canceled recruiting visit.

In approximately August 2023, a hurricane disrupted a recruit’s flight. Batie-Smoose says she returned from the airport to the gym to update Kress, who ignored her greeting twice. After she commented on his behavior, she alleges, he followed her into her office and closed the door.

The complaint says he "cornered, yelled at, and berated her" and told her he could get her fired. Batie-Smoose describes feeling physically unsafe during the encounter.

She says she reported the incident to athletics human resources and an administrator overseeing the program, but "in response, Plaintiff was told that Kress was her boss and that she needed to listen to him. Kress received no disciplinary action for his behavior towards Plaintiff."

The filing also describes alleged confrontations involving players. OutKick is not disclosing the names of the players.

The complaint alleges Kress berated one athlete "so harshly for not passing her running test that she experienced panic attacks. Plaintiff reported this mistreatment to Alexander. Upon information and belief, Kress was not disciplined."

It described another alleged incident in which a player was "excoriated by Kress in front of the team for being a few minutes late to the locker room after a losing match. The ferocity of his interaction resulted in both Plaintiff and [the player] informing Alexander about the incident. Upon information and belief, Kress was not disciplined."

The new complaint also separately cites an older accusation against Kress.

Fox News Digital reported in July that a former Fairfield player had accused Kress of a 1998 hotel-room assault.

Batie-Smoose’s filing alleges that the former player notified SJSU in October 2024 and that an official acknowledged her stated safety concern. It argues that the university’s handling of that report supports her claim of disparate treatment.

"Plaintiff is further informed and believes, based on public reporting, that Defendant took no further action following this correspondence, and that Kress continued to coach and travel with the SJSU women’s volleyball team without interruption or restriction. Plaintiff alleges that Defendant’s handling of this report is consistent with, and corroborates, the pattern of disparate treatment against Plaintiff alleged throughout this Complaint," the lawsuit states.

On Oct. 29, 2024, Batie-Smoose submitted a Title IX complaint alleging unequal treatment and failures to address concerns inside the program regarding the transgender athlete and the female players on that year's team. Days later, the university placed her on paid administrative leave.

According to her new lawsuit, her punishment arrived on Nov. 2, about 90 minutes before a home match: a university administrator blocked her entry to the gym, required her to surrender her identification and keys, and instructed her to leave. She alleges she could not retrieve belongings from her office. The filing includes an attachment of her suspension letter.

The letter referenced a complaint against Batie-Smoose dated Oct. 24 — five days before her own Title IX submission. The allegations included differential treatment based on a protected status, disclosure of confidential student information, drinking with athletes during team travel, unprofessional or insubordinate conduct, inappropriate language and a failure or refusal to coach athletes.

The letter prohibited campus access and contact with student-athletes and imposed restrictions on discussing the investigation, with exceptions including legal counsel and a union representative.

Batie-Smoose alleges the university used the accusations as a pretext and enforced its rules differently against her than against Kress.

She denies improperly disclosing protected education records and says the information she discussed came from public sources or personal observations.

Batie-Smoose acknowledged having a drink in an airport lounge while adult players were present, but says she neither purchased their drinks nor encouraged them to drink. She alleges another male coach was drinking there without facing the same consequences.

She also denies directing inappropriate language at players or refusing to coach an athlete for whom she had responsibility.

On Jan. 31, 2025, athletics director Jeff Konya notified her that her temporary coaching appointment would not be renewed, in a letter issued on behalf of President Cynthia Teniente-Matson.

Batie-Smoose's latest lawsuit was filed Oct. 13 in the Northern District of California, the lawsuit names the California State University trustees and 11 university employees, including Kress, after a legal setback in September.

On Sept. 4, Judge Noël Wise dismissed Batie-Smoose’s previous amended complaint, which asserted discrimination and retaliation under Title VII and Title IX.

Wise found that the allegations did not plausibly connect the suspension or nonrenewal to Batie-Smoose’s sex or protected advocacy. The order emphasized the complaint’s account that the university acted after she disclosed student information to the media despite instructions to keep it confidential.

"Plaintiff’s complaint supports that she was disciplined for violating a confidentiality law, not for opposing discrimination on the basis of sex," Wise wrote. The ruling granted leave to amend within 21 days, so now Batie-Smoose and her attorneys have escalated their fight with a trove of new allegations.

SJSU and CSU have declined to provide responses to Batie-Smoose's latest complaint.

INSIDE THE FALLOUT OF THE SJSU VOLLEYBALL SCANDAL: ‘THIS IS AN OBVIOUS PROBLEM’

"Due to pending litigation, San Jose State is unable to comment," an SJSU spokesperson told OutKick.

A CSU spokesperson responded, writing, "The CSU is not commenting at this time. We were made aware of the lawsuit yesterday and are still reviewing the claims."

The new complaint comes as SJSU and CSU find themselves in the midst of a mult-front legal battle with Batie-Smoose, former athletes, and President Donald Trump's administration over the scandal.

On Jan. 28, 2026, the Education Department’s Office for Civil Rights issued a findings letter addressing SJSU’s volleyball program. The letter, attached to Batie-Smoose’s new complaint, concluded that the university violated Title IX in its treatment of athletic participation, sex-separated facilities and the handling of discrimination complaints.

On employment and scholarships, the letter expressed compliance concerns and identified evidence it considered indicative of unequal treatment, while acknowledging gaps in the records.

Some of the most consequential passages concern the university’s handling of its two coaches.

OCR reported that personnel investigations involving Batie-Smoose and Kress were opened on Nov. 12, 2024, and questioned why the university suspended her but not him. The letter cited investigator notes stating that Kress "crossed the FERPA line in his interview with ESPN," referring to the federal student privacy law.

The letter also described internal records suggesting officials worried that suspending Kress could "spark more media attention" and "unduly disrupt the team."

The lawsuit, citing those passages, argues that privacy and team stability were applied selectively.

CSU disputes that comparison. Its March complaint against the Education Department argues that the coaches were not similarly situated, that Batie-Smoose disclosed protected information, and that an investigation found insufficient evidence that Kress retaliated against Slusser. The system also challenges the federal investigation’s procedures and conclusions.

Meanwhile, CSU’s disagreement with Washington has become a lawsuit of its own.

The university system sued the Education Department on March 6, arguing that the government was attempting to punish SJSU retroactively for conduct consistent with the law, federal guidance and NCAA rules in effect during the 2022–24 seasons.

CSU declined the federal government’s proposed resolution agreement. It maintains that protecting transgender students and complying with then-governing rules did not amount to unlawful sex discrimination.

Federal officials threatened enforcement that could put funding at risk. But a March 31 court order established protections against funding disruption based on the challenged findings.

The legal landscape has also changed since the 2024 season.

On Feb. 6, 2025, the NCAA changed its policy to restrict competition on women’s teams to athletes assigned female at birth, following Trump’s executive order the previous day. The policy permits athletes assigned male at birth to practice with women’s teams under specified conditions.

On June 30, 2026, the Supreme Court upheld the challenged restrictions in West Virginia and Idaho, ruling that Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause permit schools to reserve female teams based on biological sex.

The court expressly left unresolved a separate question: whether schools may allow transgender women and girls to participate on female teams. That limitation matters in the SJSU dispute, where permission to exclude and a legal obligation to exclude are different issues.

In March, a Colorado federal judge dismissed the Mountain West defendants from the lawsuit brought by Slusser, Batie-Smoose and other volleyball players. The court found that the conference was not subject to Title IX and was not a state actor for the constitutional claims. It also dismissed several claims against university officials, while deferring a ruling on Title IX damages claims against the CSU trustees pending the Supreme Court’s decision. Supplemental briefing continued after that decision.

For Batie-Smoose, the latest suit seeks both compensation and restoration of her professional standing.

She requests reinstatement to her former job or a comparable position, back pay and other compensatory relief, punitive damages against individually liable defendants, legal fees and a jury trial. She also asks for removal or correction of adverse personnel records, including the suspension letter, the later evaluation and an October 2025 nondiscrimination-policy finding. The complaint specifies no total damages figure.

She has returned to coaching elsewhere. Cisco College announced her appointment as head volleyball coach in April.

But her new filing asks a court to revisit the place she left: the gym entrance where she says her work was interrupted, the personnel file that followed, and the university decisions that she alleges converted a dispute over women’s sports into the loss of her job.

CSU has disputed the broader accusations against SJSU. In its own litigation against the Department of Education, the university system says it followed the law and athletic eligibility rules applicable during the seasons at issue, protected student privacy and investigated complaints.

It also says an investigation found that Batie-Smoose discriminated against Blaire Fleming because of sex and gender identity. Batie-Smoose contests the university’s findings and denies refusing to coach any athlete.

item.title: Minneapolis progressives turn on George Floyd-era public safety overhaul, push to dismantle office
item.description: Minneapolis Council leaders propose eliminating the Office of Community Safety over audit failures and wasteful spending, and Mayor Jacob Frey pushes back.
item.content:encoded:
Minneapolis City Council leaders advanced a proposal Tuesday to eliminate the city's Office of Community Safety as part of a sweeping public safety restructuring, citing poor management and financial oversight concerns.

Mayor Jacob Frey warned the move could jeopardize critical services. 

According to The Star Tribune, the office was created by Mayor Frey in 2022 in response to calls for police reform after the death of George Floyd.

3 DEAD, INCLUDING SUSPECTED GUNMAN, AND 3 OFFICERS INJURED IN MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING

City Council President Elliott Payne and Council Member Robin Wonsley, who are spearheading the measure to eliminate the office, cited performance and cost concerns in a statement to FOX 9.

"It is good governance to stop investing in things that are not producing meaningful outcomes and are wasting taxpayer dollars," Wonsley said. "The Office of Community Safety has also contributed to increased audit costs due to poor management. It’s our responsibility to cut unnecessary bureaucracy that does not contribute to public safety."

The proposal marks a significant reversal for a city that reorganized public safety operations after Floyd's death. Frey, who established the office in 2022, criticized council members for seeking to dismantle a structure some had previously championed. In a statement to Fox News Digital, the mayor warned that the proposed elimination could threaten existing public safety programs.

"This office — one that these council members advocated for — manages services like mental health response, violence prevention and police reform. If council members want these services in jeopardy, that’s on them. This wholesale elimination without a plan, combined with other proposed cuts to MPD, is not a serious proposal when it comes to public safety in our city," Frey said.

According to the City of Minneapolis, the Office of Community Safety oversees five departments: police, fire, 911, emergency management and neighborhood safety. The office was designed to coordinate public safety services, improve communication between departments and establish a unified chain of command and accountability.

GOP ACCUSES WALZ ALLIES OF BURYING $52M MEDICAID FRAUD REPORT BEFORE ELECTION

The proposal comes amid mounting scrutiny of the city's violence prevention spending. A recent Minneapolis audit identified serious deficiencies in the Neighborhood Safety Department's oversight of community-based violence prevention contracts, including inadequate documentation and financial controls that increased the risk of fraud and misuse of taxpayer money.

According to the investigation, the city failed to properly oversee millions of dollars awarded to violence prevention organizations. The audit examined a system that has directed more than $36 million to five major violence prevention programs since 2023.

WALZ ADMINISTRATION IGNORED FRAUD WARNINGS AS BILLIONS VANISHED, HOUSE OVERSIGHT REPORT ALLEGES

Payne defended the proposed restructuring as a way to preserve services while reducing administrative expenses.

"These proposed changes to the government structure ensure that progress on issues such as public safety and racial disparities is not impacted by unnecessary costs and bureaucratic bottlenecks," Payne told FOX 9.

"Now more than ever, our city government must be responsive to the needs of residents, and its structure should reflect that."

The city's published 2026 public safety budget allocated more than $16 million to the Office of Community Safety, nearly $10 million to Neighborhood Safety and more than $225 million to the Minneapolis Police Department. It remains unclear how much money eliminating the office would actually save.

Wonsley defended the proposal in comments to Fox News Digital, explaining that key non-police programs that continue to show success, such as the Behavioral Crisis Response team, predated the Office of Community Safety and would continue to operate without it.

"The Office of Community Safety became administrative bloat that was a barrier to creating and expanding alternative responses rather than leading the development of a comprehensive public safety system," Wonsley said. She argued the $2 million office had become a "bureaucratic barrier" plagued by mismanagement by Mayor Frey and said taxpayers have paid the price.

"The city can advance a comprehensive safety system and support police reform much more efficiently without unnecessary bureaucratic layers that have proven to be ineffective," Wonsley added. 

"Residents should not anticipate negative impacts because OCS was never able to effectively manage or oversee programs and services. The proposal does not eliminate any violence prevention or public safety programs that produce results. It simply removes administrative bloat."

item.title: Tomi Lahren suggests Tony Romo to listen to the advice he gave her during 2016 Trevor Noah backlash
item.description: Tomi Lahren revealed Tony Romo once gave her advice about handling online hate, words the former Dallas Cowboys signal caller now needs himself.
item.content:encoded:
Former NFL quarterback Tony Romo's life has been a bit of a roller coaster these days.

The four-time Pro Bowl selection recently parted ways with CBS, citing the need to take a mental health break.

This came just a few short months after he was arrested on charges of OWI in Wisconsin back in July, and happened the same day he was booted from the Korn Ferry qualifier for signing an incorrect scorecard.

It's probably safe to say that 2026 has not been Romo's year, but if anyone knows how to handle rough times amid public scrutiny, it's the former Dallas Cowboys signal-caller.

JIM NANTZ SPEAKS OUT ON 'GREAT FRIEND' TONY ROMO'S OWI ARREST, SAYS HE WILL 'ALWAYS' BE THERE FOR HIM

And OutKick's very own Tomi Lahren has proof.

During an episode of "Tomi Lahren is Fearless," Lahren explained to her guest, Barstool's Kevin "KFC" Clancy, that Romo once offered up some sage advice about dealing with online hate.

"It was actually Tony Romo at the time who told me, 'you think the whole world is talking about it, but really, nobody is,'" Lahren recounts.

This came on the heels of Lahren receiving some hateful comments for her appearance on "The Daily Show with Trevor Noah" just after Donald Trump won in 2016.

"Basically the message was, 'don't be so full of yourself that you think that everybody is talking about you,'" Lahren relayed. "Because most people aren't even on the internet."

Clancy concurred and took things even one step further.

"I think humans are not meant to be this connected and interact this much," he opined. "We can't handle it."

The longtime Barstool employee goes on to explain that for 99.9% of human history, we as humans were only confined to interacting with our small community.

COWBOYS OWNER JERRY JONES HAS TONY ROMO'S BACK, BELIEVES HE WILL 'WORK THROUGH' OWI ARREST

"The fact that you have access to millions of people's opinions ... I don't think we are even wired to be able to handle that."

It's great advice from all parties involved, and Romo would be wise to heed the words he offered up to Lahren nearly a decade ago.

He's going through a rough patch, but he will come out on the other side.

A guy as resilient as Romo is — undrafted from a small school in Eastern Illinois, coming back from a number of injuries — will be able to rebound just fine.

No one knows what the future holds for the former CBS commentator, but as for the noise online in the present, 46-year-old Romo just needs to listen to the 36-year-old version of himself.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"You think the whole world is talking about it, but really, nobody is."

item.title: DOJ threatens emergency legal action against California over suspected noncitizen voters
item.description: The Justice Department threatens emergency legal action against California over suspected noncitizens on voter rolls ahead of midterm elections.
item.content:encoded:
The Justice Department is threatening emergency legal action against California election officials unless they take steps to prevent suspected noncitizens from voting in November's midterm elections, setting a Thursday deadline as state officials push back.

In letters sent Tuesday, Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter demanded that California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan review a list of potentially ineligible voters within 48 hours. The DOJ instructed officials to segregate ballots from individuals whose citizenship cannot be verified and warned it would seek emergency legal relief if its demands were not met by noon Eastern on Oct. 15.

A DOJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital that thousands of potential foreign nationals ineligible to vote have been identified on California's voter rolls statewide, not just in Los Angeles County.

MAP IT: DOJ ILLEGAL VOTING CRACKDOWN SWEEPS 17 STATES AS RAZOR-THIN ELECTIONS FACE SCRUTINY

"This should not be controversial, as the criminal statute is clear: only American citizens may vote in federal elections. It is a federal crime for noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections, and the DOJ is asking California to ensure that is not occurring," the spokesperson said.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, pushed back during a Wednesday news conference, accusing the Trump administration of attempting to intimidate voters and promoting false allegations of widespread voter fraud.

JUSTICE DEPARTMENT CHARGES 16 ACROSS MULTIPLE STATES WITH ALLEGED ILLEGAL VOTING, ELECTION CRIMES

"There is no widespread voter preference, voter fraud problem. It doesn't exist. It is a lie. It is a conspiracy theory," Bonta said.

Bonta said his office is working with the secretary of state and Los Angeles County officials to review their options.

STATE DEPARTMENT CONSIDERS SHARING PASSPORT RECORDS FOR VOTER CITIZENSHIP CHECKS

Meanwhile, Logan said his office received a password-protected USB drive purportedly containing voter records but has not accessed it because of cybersecurity concerns.

"We have not accessed the drive because doing so would conflict with established data privacy and information security protocols. We do not consider the device a secure medium. Additionally, the letter does not specify the number of individuals involved or describe the information contained in the records," he said.

The dispute comes as Californians are already casting ballots ahead of the Nov. 3 election. Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, though the DOJ has not established that the individuals identified have cast illegal ballots.

item.title: Fox News Poll: Cost-of-living concerns weigh on GOP in midterms
item.description: A Fox News survey finds Trump's approval on inflation hitting a new low of 22% as six in 10 voters say cost of living is their top economic worry.
item.content:encoded:
When voters rate the economy and the president negatively just weeks before Election Day, the incumbent party is vulnerable, and that’s certainly the case in the latest Fox News survey.

The economic landscape is stark. Six in 10 voters say the cost of living is their top economic worry, overshadowing government spending (15%), jobs and income inequality (7% each), tariffs (6%) and taxes (5%). 

Majorities rate the economy negatively (74%) and expect it to worsen next year (53%), while two-thirds are dissatisfied with how things are going in the country (66%). Few, 18%, say their family is better off compared to two years ago. Independents say they’re worse off (52%) and think the economy will get worse (70%).

FOX NEWS POLL: IT’S A LONE STAR SENATE SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TALARICO AND PAXTON

A majority of voters, 55%, say inflation is "not at all" under control. That’s up from a low of 45% earlier this year, and includes 30% of Republicans.

President Donald Trump’s lowest job rating is on inflation: 22% approve, a new low. Last summer, 36% approved. Four years ago, before the 2022 midterms, 29% approved of former President Joe Biden’s performance on inflation.

Disapproval of the job Trump is doing has reached 77% on inflation, 70% on the economy, 69% on tariffs and 64% on foreign policy. A smaller share, but still a majority, disapprove of his handling of immigration (56% disapprove), while border security is the only issue that is close to positive (50% approve, 50% disapprove).

Trump’s overall job approval is 36%, his lowest ever in a Fox News survey for either term. It had been holding steady at 39% since May. The decline is mainly driven by decreases among voters under age 45, those with annual household income below $50,000, non-White voters, and those without a college degree.

FOX NEWS POLL: MICHIGAN VOTERS SPLIT BETWEEN EL-SAYED AND ROGERS

Approval stands at a low of 76% among Republicans. That’s down 3 points since last month, 12 points since September 2025, and 16 points since early in his second term (March 2025).

As in most midterms, voters are prone to punish the party in power: 7 in 10 say they will vote to send a message to Trump, with nearly twice as many expressing opposition (47%) as support (25%).

If the election were today, 54% of voters say they would back the Democratic candidate in their House district and 45% would support the Republican. That is outside the margin of error and is a wider lead than last month when Democrats were ahead by 51%-44%. The race narrows among those saying they are certain to vote, with the Democratic candidate ahead by 52%-46%.

The survey finds about the same number self-identify as Democrats (43%) and Republicans (41%), and both parties feel equally certain about voting (62% and 64% respectively), while more Democrats (61%) than Republicans (52%) say they are extremely interested in the election.

Party loyalty is solid: 98% of Democrats support their party’s candidate, and 94% of Republicans back theirs. Independents favor the Democrats by 26 points.

The Democratic candidate is the choice among Whites with a degree, those under age 45, women, union households and Hispanics. The Republican is ahead among Whites without a college degree (White men without a degree in particular), those 65 and over, voters who attend religious services regularly, military veterans and White evangelical Christians.

While 43% of Hispanic voters supported Trump in the 2024 election, just 31% prefer the Republican candidate this year.

"When the country is this closely divided in terms of partisanship, slight differences in defection and turnout rates can make all the difference," said Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who helps conduct the Fox News Poll with Democrat Chris Anderson. "Republicans have time to close these apparent gaps, but it’s getting late."

Meanwhile, Democrats lead on 10 out of 13 issue concerns.

The top five voter concerns are government corruption (60% extremely concerned), inflation (58%), gas prices (50%), government leadership (49%), and healthcare (48%). And double digits more trust the Democrats than the Republicans to handle each of those.

Republicans retain the advantage on crime (by 10 points) and border security (R+8), while views are closely divided on immigration (R+3). The Democrats are seen as better on healthcare (D+22), inflation (D+16), gas prices (D+12), voting rights (D+12), election integrity (D+12), government leadership (D+11), what’s taught in public schools (D+11), artificial intelligence (D+10), government corruption (D+10) and foreign policy (D+9).

Republicans have lost ground on key issues compared to four years ago, when more voters trusted them by 21 points on border security, 13 points on inflation and 9 points on foreign policy.

Other issues that voters are extremely concerned about are the Iran war (42%), immigration (35%), crime (34%), voter suppression (32%), AI technology (32%), what’s taught in public schools (29%), voter fraud (28%) and border security (25%).

While corruption in government and inflation are the top two worries about both parties, far more Democrats (72% and 70%) than Republicans (47% and 49%) are extremely concerned.

The issue that helps explain the Democrats’ advantage isn’t an issue at all. By a 14-point margin, more voters think the Democrats will do a better job "fighting for people like you." Majorities of White voters with a college degree (53%), men (52%), women (60%) and non-White voters (77%) think Democrats will fight for them. Whites without a college degree are split 49-49%.

Despite their issue advantage, just 35% say Democrats have a clear plan for dealing with the country’s problems, and 33% say the same about the Republicans. That reverses the Republican advantage from July 2025, when 43% said the Republicans had a clear plan compared with 33% for the Democrats.

There’s deep dissatisfaction with lawmakers: 15% approve of Congress, while 84% disapprove. Remarkably, that’s above the low of 9% approval in October 2013.

Both parties are viewed negatively. The Democratic Party is underwater by 16 points (42% favorable, 58% unfavorable), while ratings of the GOP are net negative by 23 points (38% favorable, 61% unfavorable).

Yet, favorable ratings fail to translate directly into vote choice. One third of those backing the Democratic candidate (31%) dislike the party, while 23% of those supporting the Republican dislike the GOP. Among the 26% who dislike both parties (double haters), Democrats lead 62%-36%.

Here’s how polarized the parties are: Just 16% of Republicans say that Democrats love America and want what’s best for the U.S., and even fewer Democrats, 6%, think Republicans do.

Compared to four years ago, the number of voters saying Democrats want what’s best for the country is up four points, while fewer say Republicans love the country now by 6 points.

Fifty-one percent of voters have a favorable view of capitalism compared with 32% for socialism. Compared to a year ago, positive ratings of capitalism are down 2 points while they are up 5 points for socialism. Eight in ten of those with a positive view of socialism support the Democratic candidate, while 6 in 10 of those viewing capitalism favorably back the Republican.

Voters who plan to cast their ballots early favor the Democratic candidate (by 19 points) as do mail voters (D+33), while the candidate choice splits among those voting in person (early or on Election Day).

Six in 10 oppose U.S. military action against Iran, and they back the Democrats by 56 points.

CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE

A new high of 46% think the U.S. is too supportive of Israel, and those voters favor the Democratic candidate by 42 points, while the 4 in 10 who think U.S. support of Israel is about right pick the Republican by 27 points.

Nearly 6 in 10 have a negative view of artificial intelligence technology, and they back the Democratic candidate by 27 points.

Conducted Oct. 9-12, 2026, under the direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News survey includes interviews with a sample of 1,202 registered voters randomly selected from a national voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (114) and cellphones (786) or completed the survey online after receiving a text (302). Results based on the full sample have a margin of sampling error of ±2.5 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling errors, question wording and order can influence results. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education and area variables to ensure the demographics are representative of the registered voter population. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis and voter file data.

Fox News’ Victoria Balara contributed to this report.

item.title: Expert calls California 'Wild West' for surrogacy after couple charged with abusing surrogate-born children
item.description: Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang allegedly abused surrogate-born children while running an unlicensed California surrogacy agency from their home.
item.content:encoded:
The case of a California couple recently accused of abusing children born to surrogates exposes the pitfalls of an industry one expert described as the "wild west."

Guojun Xuan, 66, and his wife, Silvia Zhang, 39, were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit child abuse. Authorities said the couple operated their own surrogacy agency out of their home in Arcadia, California.

"I say it all the time. It's the wild, Wild West," Kallie Fell, executive director of the Center for Bioethics and Culture, told Fox News Digital.

SURROGATE WHO REFUSED ABORTION TAKES FIGHT TO SUPREME COURT AS BABY'S LIFE HANGS IN BALANCE

Xuan and Zhang allegedly abused more than a dozen surrogate-born children — some as young as 2 months old — inside their multimillion-dollar Arcadia residence.

Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman called the alleged abuse "appalling and revolting."

OHIO MOM OF 16 CRADLES STOMACH IN COURT, PLEADS NOT GUILTY IN SEVERE ABUSE CASE INVOLVING OWN CHILDREN

"This was not a home where these children were loved and nurtured," Hochman said when announcing the charges. "This was a home where these young children were systematically beaten and punished if they did not do what they were told."

In addition to the alleged abuse, the couple operated Future Spring Surrogacy from their home, recruiting surrogates and paying them tens of thousands of dollars. At least eight surrogates reported aggressive tactics and false statements regarding the family's living situation, officials said.

SURROGATE WHO REFUSED ABORTION ASKS SCOTUS TO INTERVENE AS BABY COULD BE MOVED OUT OF TEXAS

"The thing about the case is that I wish it was shocking for me," said Fell, who opposes commercial surrogacy. "Because of the space I work in, I get to hear shocking stories around the globe — things that people don't realize the surrogacy industry has grown into. It's not just a place where couples who have been struggling with infertility go as a last resort to have a child."

"I mean, this has really turned into, if you have enough money to pay for it, then you can, by any means necessary, really have a child in California," she added.

SURROGATE, CALIFORNIA COUPLE CLASH IN COURT AS NEWBORN FIGHTS FOR LIFE AFTER HEART SURGERY

Unlike in some states, a license is not required in California to open a surrogacy agency, and there is no comprehensive regulatory framework to oversee the industry across the state.

Surrogacy is a billion-dollar global market used to help couples who are unable to conceive or carry a child. The issue, Fell noted, is that while the process is accessible to anyone who can afford it, there are no meaningful regulatory safeguards for the children born to surrogates.

"I was a foster parent," she said. "My husband and I went through gobs of courses, gobs of home studies, background checks, everything — really under a microscope. The same is not true for surrogacy. It doesn't apply."

As the surrogacy boom has expanded, foreign nationals — many from China — have increasingly used American surrogates to have children, according to a 2024 report by the Heritage Foundation.

Because commercial surrogacy is completely illegal inside China, wealthy Chinese individuals and couples frequently look abroad, primarily to the U.S., to grow their families.

While banned or heavily restricted in several other countries, cross-border surrogacy is not regulated at the federal level in the U.S., opening the door for foreign clients to secure American birthright citizenship for the resulting children, according to the conservative think tank.

"We absolutely need to close our borders to international surrogacy," Fell said. "Why do we need folks from overseas coming, renting wombs here in the United States?"

item.title: Wildlife influencer comes close to losing a wrestling match to a 19-foot reticulated python
item.description: Mike Holston, known as The Real Tarzann, nearly lost his toughest battle yet when a 19-foot reticulated python wrapped his arm and both legs.
item.content:encoded:
A wildlife influencer who goes by the name The Real Tarzann on social media put his blue belt jiu-jitsu skills up against a 19-foot reticulated python. Smart.

He realizes he's getting dangerously close to being in trouble when the snake wraps up one of his arms and both of his legs at the same time.

After having the python strike towards him a couple of times, he grabs its head and is in for his "toughest battle with a snake yet."

MMA FIGHTER CONFIDENTLY BELIEVES HE CAN BEAT A CHIMPANZEE IN A FIGHT AND CLAIMS IT WILL BE LIVESTREAMED

item.title: Bear breaks into Alaska hospital at 2 am, helps itself to an early Halloween candy buffet

item.content:encoded:

So there she was, trapped in a hallway with a hungry black bear.

Warnke slowly backed away, hoping the bear hadn't noticed her. Fortunately, that's when our furry friend discovered the candy bucket and apparently decided chocolate was better than human.

Eventually, an announcement came over the hospital intercom warning everyone that there was a bear in the building. But that didn't stop some doctors from coming out to take pictures.

Warnke made it out safely, and the bear reportedly exited through the same entrance he'd used to get inside. Nobody was injured.

item.title: Michael Penix Jr likely starting for Falcons against Bears despite rib injury, Kevin Stefanski says
item.description: Michael Penix Jr. left Sunday's game with a rib injury and was replaced by Tua Tagovailoa in overtime, but he's set to start against Chicago.
item.content:encoded:
The quarterback situation in Atlanta has been one of the NFL’s most closely watched storylines. After an offseason marked by injuries and a two-week stint with Cooper Rush under center, Atlanta appeared to find some stability when Michael Penix Jr. returned to the starting lineup.

Late in Sunday’s hard-fought game against the Baltimore Ravens, Penix sustained a rib injury on a sack. He briefly returned before the end of regulation but could not continue in overtime, forcing Tua Tagovailoa to take over.

Tagovailoa threw the game-ending interception, leaving Penix’s status for a pivotal Week 6 meeting with the Chicago Bears uncertain.

After Penix underwent an MRI earlier this week, Falcons coach Kevin Stefanski said Wednesday that the quarterback is on track to start Sunday’s game, barring any setbacks.

Penix was back at practice Wednesday, although he was listed as a limited participant.

BACKUP QUARTERBACK TYLER HUNTLEY LEADS BALTIMORE RAVENS TO IMPROBABLE OT WIN OVER ATLANTA FALCONS

Stefanski stopped short of offering details about what he knew about the extent of Penix's rib injury, instead telling reporters that the left-handed thrower is "feeling better."

On Monday, ESPN’s Adam Schefter told "The Pat McAfee Show" that Penix’s rib injury "didn’t look like it’s a long-term injury" at the time.

Penix’s practice workload this week will depend on how he feels, Stefanski said.

"I want to see how he's feeling," Stefanski said. "With any injury like this, you want to make sure as they move around and how they're feeling -- it could be all, some, none. We shall see."

ESPN reported later on Wednesday that Penix "took all the first-team reps in practice."

"I felt good today at practice," Penix told reporters when asked the status of his ribs. "… I just gotta stay on top of my rehab and just make sure I'm doing all the right things."

He added: "I feel good to go this week, so that's the plan."

Penix’s injury history, dating back to his college days, is well documented. He suffered his latest ACL injury last November and underwent surgery. His recovery kept him out of the Falcons’ first two games this season.

Bears star Caleb Williams' status is also unclear for Sunday's game in Atlanta. He's missed the last two games with a hamstring injury. However, Bears head coach Ben Johnson said Wednesday that Williams would be listed was a full participant on the latest injury report.

item.content:encoded:
When you know, you know, and Baltimore Ravens star Kyle Hamilton certainly knew.

After the Ravens scored to take a 30-23 lead over the Atlanta Falcons in overtime on Sunday and Hamilton saw Tua Tagovailoa come onto the field, he was ebullient. He knew he was going to seal the game.

"Kyle (looked across the field) and was like, ‘Tua in the game!’" Ravens star cornerback Marlon Humphrey recalled on a recent episode of "The Marlon Humphrey Show."

"He knew he was going to get a pick. He literally was like, ‘Oh, he better throw me one.’ He was so excited, it was the most excited I’ve probably seen Kyle."

Humphrey said he didn't know if Hamilton knew something he didn't, but Hamilton was confident he would get an interception. It was Hamilton's first interception of the season and the sixth of his career.

Tagovailoa entered the game late in the fourth quarter for Michael Penix Jr., who left after taking a vicious shot to the ribs. Penix returned for one play before overtime, but after the Ravens scored in the extra period, it was the former Miami Dolphins star who led the Falcons’ offense onto the field.

The Falcons hope Penix can indeed return, because without him in the lineup, offensive production cratered. With both Penix and Tagovailoa injured to begin the season and Cooper Rush at quarterback, the offense scored just 16 points over the first two weeks of the season.

item.title: Josh Allen's sweet Hailee Steinfeld moment caught on camera after the Bills' thrilling overtime win
item.description: Josh Allen searched SoFi Stadium suites for wife Hailee Steinfeld after the Buffalo Bills' thrilling 37-34 overtime win over the Los Angeles Rams.
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles is full of stars, but after the Buffalo Bills' win on Monday, Josh Allen was only looking for one: his wife.

Allen was seen walking off the field after the Bills’ thrilling 37-34 overtime victory over the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium, looking up into the stands for "Sinners" star Hailee Steinfeld.

"Is my wife in one of these suites somewhere?" Allen asked in a video captured by Spectrum News 1.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"Does anybody know?"

While the MVP-winning quarterback seemed unable to find Steinfeld, she was shown passionately cheering for her husband during the "Monday Night Football" broadcast.

"Go, Josh! Let’s go, Josh! Let’s f---ing go!" Steinfeld was seen yelling during the game.

Steinfeld had every reason to be engrossed in the game, as the Bills and Rams scored a combined 48 points in a captivating second half that required overtime. However, for a moment in the extra period, it looked like Allen was going to suffer his eighth straight overtime loss.

The Bills got the ball first and drove into Rams territory, but running back James Cook fumbled for the second time in the game and turned the ball over. The Rams needed only a field goal to win following Cook's turnover, but Harrison Mevis' potential game-winning field goal attempt was blocked by Bills linebacker Greg Rousseau.

Allen took advantage of the second chance, driving the Bills back into field goal range and setting up Tyler Bass' game-winning 45-yard field goal. With the win, Allen improved to 1-7 in overtime games.

item.title: Hochul dodges when pressed over victims of illegal immigrant crime: ‘Will you apologize?’
item.description: Bruce Blakeman pressed Kathy Hochul to apologize to families of victims killed by illegal immigrants, but the governor pivoted to ICE-related deaths.
item.content:encoded:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declined to directly apologize to the families of people killed by illegal immigrants after Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman confronted her over the issue during Tuesday night's gubernatorial debate. 

Hochul instead turned the exchange toward Americans killed by federal immigration agents.

Looking directly at Hochul as he brought up several victims, Blakeman asked what she had to say to families who will "never get to sit at another Thanksgiving dinner, never be able to open their presents on their Christmas tree.

"Will you apologize to them, and will you please return Sheridan Gorman's parents' calls to talk to you about your sanctuary policy?" he said.

NEW YORK GOVERNOR DEBATE HEATS UP AS BLAKEMAN, HOCHUL SPAR OVER TRUMP, SANCTUARY STATUS, ICE SHOOTING

Jose Medina-Medina, an illegal immigrant from Venezuela, faces charges related to the fatal shooting of Sheridan Gorman, an 18-year-old Loyola University Chicago student from Yorktown, New York, as she walked with friends near her campus late at night. 

Her death has fueled calls for change from her parents, who have taken aim at sanctuary policies that limit cooperation between local law enforcement and ICE.

Hochul responded by calling all crimes "heartbreaking," adding, "I abhor all crimes, regardless of the perpetrator."

She went on to say her administration has spent billions to "help law enforcement do their jobs" and reduce crime across the state.

SHERIDAN GORMAN’S MOM SCORCHES DEM LAWMAKERS SHE SAYS REFUSED TO HEAR FAMILIES OF SLAIN AMERICANS

"We have driven down crime to historic lows, especially violent crimes like shootings and murders, and that didn't come easy," she said. "That took a lot of work. I've had to change laws. I've got to allocate more money."

Hochul did not directly answer Blakeman's request for an apology or his question about returning Gorman's parents' calls. Instead, she brought up Renee Good and Alex Pretti, who were shot and killed during separate confrontations with federal immigration agents in Minneapolis in January.

"When you're talking about ICE, what I find so shocking is that when an American mother was murdered by ICE agents, you said that her killing was justified," she fired back.

MULLIN CALLS MAMDANI'S ANTI-ICE RHETORIC 'DANGEROUS' FOLLOWING NEW YORK SHOOTING

She said Blakeman did not have an answer when asked whether Pretti’s death was "justified," saying, "I find those answers just reprehensible, so you won't apologize. I apologize for any pain that has happened to anyone."

The exchange set off a wave of social media scrutiny, with critics accusing Hochul of not caring about the victims.

"INSANE! Kathy Hochul can’t even apologize to victims of crimes committed by illegal aliens - or promise to return their calls," RNC Research posted on X.

"She couldn't care less," radio host Brett Winterble posted on X.

"Disgusting," Republican National Committee spokesperson Kristen Cianci posted on X.

"NO APOLOGY. No ownership of the sanctuary policies," Richard Sementa, executive producer of "The Mark Levin Show," posted on X.

"BOOM! Bruce Blakeman put Kathy Hochul's immigration policies on trial, live. Bruce Blakeman: "What do you say to their families, Kathy?" Families of victims want answers, and Hochul still hasn't given them one," conservative influencer Gunther Eagleman posted on X.

Voters will decide between Hochul and Blakeman in the upcoming November election to determine who will serve as New York governor.

The Michigan Wolverines are on the cusp of dipping into the transfer portal and signing two players who could help them at multiple positions this season. Yes, I said this season.

Thanks to a temporary restraining order granted by a Washtenaw County Circuit Court Judge, former Miami Hurricanes tight end Alex Bauman and former Boise State defensive back Jeremiah Earby are now legally allowed to play this season.

SEC ACCUSES LSU OF DEFYING ITS RULES AS WILL WADE'S BASKETBALL ROSTER ADDS FUEL TO A BURNING FIRE

In fact, both are reportedly enrolled at Michigan, after a judge in the state granted them the ability to be rostered.

JUDGE GRANTS INJUNCTION AGAINST NCAA, SEC, ALLOWING ATHLETES WITH NFL TIES ELIGIBLE TO PLAY FOR LSU, OTHERS

If you're wondering how Earby and Bauman would be allowed a return to college football, based off the professional rules established by the Big Ten conference, it all hinges on the fact that neither player signed with an NFL team.

When the NCAA enacted new guidelines on how many years an athlete has to compete at the collegiate level, this spurred a plethora of lawsuits against the organization by members of the 2022 class that felt as though they were being singled out.

After playing for Boise State last season and recording 60 tackles, Jeremiah Earby did not receive an opportunity at the professional level. NFL TO NCAA? COURTROOM CHAOS IS GIVING PRO ATHLETES A BIZARRE PATH BACK TO COLLEGE, AND IT'S ONLY JUST BEGUN

For Bauman, he was a member of the Miami Hurricanes 2025 team that played for a national championship against Indiana. Before playing for Mario Cristobal, the wide receiver attended Tulane for three years, with his productive 2024 season garnering enough attention that landed him a spot at Miami.

item.title: Trump scores win from liberal-leaning 9th Circuit in ICE enforcement showdown
item.description: The 9th Circuit ruled the Trump administration is "certain to succeed" against California's No Vigilantes Act, dealing a blow to Gavin Newsom.
item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration scored a victory at a liberal-leaning appeals court Wednesday, which temporarily blocked a section of a California law requiring plainclothes federal law enforcement agents to show their badges and identification when carrying out operations.

The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled the Trump administration was "certain to succeed" in its lawsuit against California, finding that the No Vigilantes Act’s identification requirement violates the Constitution’s supremacy clause, which says federal law takes priority when it conflicts with state law.

"Section 10 explicitly overrides the federal government’s power to determine whether, how, and when to publicly identify its officers," the panel wrote.

The preliminary injunction comes from a federal appeals court that has repeatedly clashed with the Trump administration over some of its signature immigration policies, including blocking efforts to withhold federal funding from sanctuary cities in 2018, restricting attempts to tighten asylum eligibility that same year and refusing to reinstate Trump's travel ban targeting several predominantly Muslim countries in 2017.

FEDERAL COURT BLOCKS NEWSOM’S BID TO SHACKLE ICE IN TRUMP IMMIGRATION WIN

The ruling comes as a major blow to California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, widely viewed as a 2028 presidential hopeful. Newsom has positioned himself as a leading opponent of Trump's immigration agenda, signing a series of laws aimed at protecting immigrant communities, restricting federal immigration enforcement operations and increasing oversight of federal agents in the state.

The Trump administration sued California over provisions in the No Vigilantes Act and No Secret Police Act, which restricts law enforcement officers from wearing face coverings, in November 2025. Judge Christina Snyder, a Clinton-appointed judge, initially blocked the No Secret Police Act's mask restriction for federal officers but declined to block the No Vigilantes Act's identification requirement.

The Trump administration appealed Snyder's decision on the identification requirement, and the 9th Circuit temporarily blocked its enforcement in February before granting an injunction pending appeal in April.

FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS NEW YORK LAW BANNING ICE AGENTS FROM WEARING MASKS

California argued that its identification requirement did not amount to an unconstitutional regulation of the federal government because a state law crosses that line only when it "impose[s] substantial burdens on federal operations."

But the appeals court ruled that the state never had the authority to directly regulate federal officials.

"The burden of the regulation on federal operations, whether substantial or otherwise, is irrelevant," the court wrote.

The liberal appeals court ruling drew praise from Trump administration officials, including Brett Shumate, assistant attorney general for the Justice Department's Civil Division.

DOJ WARNS FORMER RED STATE IS BECOMING THE NEXT CALIFORNIA AS GOVERNOR EMBRACES ICE LIMITS

"The Ninth Circuit agrees that California cannot regulate federal law enforcement," Schumate wrote on X.

"Today, the Ninth Circuit again affirms what common sense makes clear: California cannot regulate how Federal law enforcement officers carry out their jobs authorized by Congress," Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, Jr. wrote on X. 

"Today's decision is a huge WIN for protecting the safety of our Nation's law enforcement officers and ensuring @POTUS 's promise to enforce our Nation's immigration laws."

Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment.

item.title: Carolina Panthers lineman Taylor Moton overcame bloody, life-threatening episode and now he's back at practice
item.description: Taylor Moton describes coughing up blood and the terrifying discovery of multiple clots in his right lung that put his life at serious risk.
item.content:encoded:
This is a comeback story of the highest order because Taylor Moton's life was at risk, blood was splattered all over his chest, and doctors frantically rushed to keep him from dying from a life-threatening emergency.

Moton is a Carolina Panthers offensive lineman.

Except, he hasn't been an offensive lineman since the offseason because he was exclusively a patient trying to overcome the condition that caused, as he put it, "a multitude of clots in my right lung."

DEION SANDERS DECLARES HE'S CANCER-FREE, ADDRESSES INCONTINENCE AHEAD OF COLORADO FOOTBALL SEASON

People die from runaway blood clots.

I had a friend die from blood clots in 2022. Miami Dolphins senior vice president Jason Jenkins died from a bilateral pulmonary thromboembolism due to phlebothrombosis. He was in his office at the team's training facility when it happened.

Jenkins had complained of the pain clots in his legs caused him for months before that. He talked about how he had to be careful when he flew because that could impact his condition.

So when Moton was placed on the non-football injury list in July it caught my attention because there had been reports about it being tied to clots since June. And that was extremely worrisome.

But this column isn't all about sadness and concern. Or death.

HOUSTON TEXANS STAR PRACTICES IN PADS FOR FIRST TIME IN NEARLY TWO YEARS AFTER 2024 CAREER-THREATENING INJURY

That's because Moton is back on the Panthers practice field this week. And he was in the locker room on Tuesday talking about his victory over a life-threatening condition.

"I was just hanging out about to take a nap, lay down, and all of sudden it started to feel like my chest was really congested," Moton told a group of reporters gathered at his locker. "I thought it was just normal chest congestion. But I started to taste blood in my mouth and then I knew something was up."

One can only imagine what a world-class athlete who hadn't yet reached his 32nd birthday thinks when confronted with a serious medical emergency. These guys train to feel invincible.

But Moton immediately realized he wasn't invincible. He was in deep trouble.

"I started coughing up blood -- and it was like a lot of it," Moton said. "And I could start feeling it leaking through my chest even -- something like really different. So, after 15-or-something minutes, I was like 'Yeah, I've got to go to the hospital.'

"Went to the hospital, they were doing CT scans, ultrasounds, trying to find what was going on. And that's when they found a multitude of clots in my right lung."

Stunning.

Moton said doctors to this day have not figured out what caused the frightening episode.

"They put me on blood thinners, and other than that I was just working," he said. "I just couldn't have contact on the blood thinners because having contact on blood thinners can lead to like a brain bleed."

Moton has been trying to stay in shape but it clearly isn't football shape. So he has 21 days to try to reach that kind of physical conditioning before a decision on his season's availability has to be made. The Panthers, dealing with injuries on their offensive line, need him as soon as possible.

The man they're getting back has a different outlook than the one who last played a game in the 2025 season.

"When you see the blood, you start thinking the worst," Moton said. "But thank God I'm still on this side of Earth, right? Like past football, man, it makes you count your blessings to be here. Still get to see my family. It's a blessing."

item.title: DOJ unveils nationwide tax fraud crackdown involving 76 defendants, nearly $500M in alleged losses
item.description: The Justice Department's first-ever National Tax Enforcement Surge targeted 76 defendants across 35 U.S. attorneys' offices in a six-week crackdown.
item.content:encoded:
The Justice Department announced a nationwide tax fraud crackdown Wednesday involving 76 defendants and more than $490 million in estimated intended tax losses, including new charges against 31 individuals accused of schemes targeting American taxpayers.

The first-ever National Tax Enforcement Surge brought together 35 U.S. attorneys' offices and IRS criminal investigators over approximately six weeks. The operation resulted in 23 new charging actions involving more than $350 million in alleged intended tax losses, while another 45 defendants were involved in trials, guilty pleas and sentencings associated with nearly $140 million in estimated intended losses.

"Every dollar stolen through tax fraud is a dollar taken from the American people," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a news release "What we uncovered during this concentrated surge is only the tip of the iceberg. The Department of Justice is committed to expanding our investigations and exposing schemes designed to evade accountability, because there is no safe haven for fraudsters."

AG BLANCHE UNVEILS FEDERAL CHARGES AGAINST 160 DEFENDANTS IN PANDEMIC RELIEF SWEEP

Speaking at Wednesday's news conference, IRS Criminal Investigation chief Jarod Koopman described the operation as a new enforcement strategy and said similar crackdowns would follow.

"The consolidated actions we are announcing today represent an entirely new approach in our enforcement strategy. Partnering with DOJ to strategically surge resources around a broad range of tax crimes. And although this type of enforcement is the first of its kind, it will not be the last," Koopman said.

APPEALS COURT UPHOLDS ORDER BLOCKING IRS FROM SHARING TAXPAYER DATA WITH ICE

Among the largest cases highlighted was an alleged fraudulent trust scheme in Texas, where four defendants were charged with promoting tax shelters that prosecutors say concealed more than $1.5 billion in income and caused over $200 million in estimated tax losses.

In Georgia, three Mexican citizens were indicted in connection with an alleged $74 million tax refund scheme involving more than 16,000 U.S. Treasury checks. Prosecutors allege the defendants used Mexican identification documents belonging to other individuals to obtain IRS taxpayer identification numbers and file fraudulent returns.

FBI OPERATION TARGETS SCAM COMPOUNDS IN AFRICA WITH ARRESTS, ACCOUNT TAKEDOWNS

Asked during the news conference how much money taxpayers could expect to recover, Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald acknowledged that fraudulent proceeds are sometimes spent before investigators can retrieve them.

McDonald said the Justice Department is building an asset forfeiture and recovery team to pursue assets allegedly purchased with fraud proceeds, including luxury vehicles and real estate. He did not provide a total recovery figure, noting that some cases remain in their early stages.

The crackdown follows the Justice Department's establishment of its National Fraud Enforcement Division in April. Defendants facing criminal charges are presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

item.title: Elle Duncan makes a fool of herself saying she and Black women are the real victims of the WNBA discourse
item.description: Elle Duncan calls WNBA discourse toxic and claims Black women are targeted, but her own career at ESPN and now Netflix tells a different story.
item.content:encoded:
Former ESPN anchor Elle Duncan called the discourse surrounding the WNBA "toxic as hell" and claimed that Black women are the target.

"It feels like open season to dunk on Black women because we do not have protection. Because no one cares. Because we are low-hanging fruit," Duncan said of the WNBA discourse during a discussion with Front Office Sports on Tuesday.

"It is very easy to dunk on us since we are, I would say, outside of transgender people, the most marginalized of the marginalized groups."

FORMER ESPN ANCHOR SMEARS CAITLIN CLARK FANS WITH SWEEPING, FALSE ACCUSATIONS OF RACISM | MATT CALKINS

Duncan, a highly peculiar individual, then accused "opportunists" of latching on to Caitlin Clark as a means of diminishing Black and queer women.

"It’s twofold for them—so you get to lift this one person up, and you get to, ultimately, reduce everybody else that isn’t her to nothing," Duncan said.

At this point, you probably expect us to respond to the examples Duncan provided to support her claims about Black women in America and the WNBA. Unfortunately, we cannot. Duncan didn't provide any.

On the surface, I reject her premise.

She says Black women lack protection, yet her own career suggests otherwise.

ESPN hired Duncan after she was arrested for driving under the influence (DUI) in April 2013. She then repeatedly used ESPN's sports programming to make personal political statements.

She reportedly lobbied behind the scenes to have the company remove Sage Steele from a social justice special in 2020 over concerns about Steele's "Blackness," whatever that means. Steele was removed.

On at least two occasions, Duncan interrupted the network's sports coverage to protest legislation.

She first called for a moment of silence in response to Florida's so-called "Don't Say Gay" bill. She later used the SportsCenter set to condemn the Supreme Court's decision to return abortion policy to the states, calling on fathers to support their daughters' ability to obtain abortions.

Last year, she again ventured into political commentary on ESPN, declaring that "everyone" should adore and love former first lady Michelle Obama. Imagine the reaction if an ESPN anchor had instructed viewers that "everyone" should adore and love first lady Melania Trump.

Yet ESPN did not discipline Duncan or distance itself from her commentary, as it did Steele after she discussed political and social issues in 2021.

By that standard, Duncan appeared quite protected at ESPN.

Despite all of that, Netflix has since hired her to anchor its sports coverage. Talk about privilege.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

I also reject the notion that Black women lack protection in the WNBA, a league composed predominantly of black women.

Recently, A'ja Wilson charged aggressively toward a fan in the stands and avoided a suspension. DiJonai Carrington also avoided discipline after clotheslining Sophie Cunningham this summer and later accusing the WNBA of racism on social media from the locker room.

Black women are also routinely afforded the benefit of the doubt by the media during WNBA controversies. ESPN's primary WNBA studio show features an all-black female panel and has often drawn criticism for holding Clark to a different standard than black players.

Further, it's difficult to take Duncan seriously when she laments the toxicity surrounding WNBA coverage. Duncan was among the media figures who helped politicize the league when Clark arrived.

She was initially ESPN's lead WNBA host, but was hardly a neutral observer. Duncan repeatedly shamed Clark over the supposed racism of anonymous online trolls, as if Clark were somehow responsible for them.

She has continued to stoke the same divisions since joining Netflix.

This summer, Duncan suggested Clark bore some responsibility for a wildly inappropriate USA Today column in which the author invoked Emmett Till while warning that Clark's silence in the face of online criticism could endanger black women.

The racialization of the WNBA has never been particularly difficult to trace. Most people have been afraid to say where much of it originated.

Clark is a straight White woman from Iowa who entered a predominantly black league with a level of fame no WNBA player had ever possessed. Players and media figures, many of whom were Black women, met her arrival with unmistakable resentment.

Some explicitly attributed her popularity to white privilege. Others invoked the "great White hope" trope to explain her appeal.

Elle Duncan, A'ja Wilson, DiJonai Carrington, Angel Reese, Monica McNutt, Cindy Brunson, Chiney Ogwumike, Sheryl Swoopes, and others are not innocent bystanders to the toxic WNBA discourse they now condemn. They have been among its most prominent participants.

In many of the controversies that have defined the league's culture war, they have been the aggressors, not the targets.

Duncan and others now want to reverse that sequence of events. They want the backlash against their own divisive rhetoric and behavior to serve as proof that black women were the victims all along.

That's a convenient revision of what actually happened.

WNBA discourse is "toxic as hell" in large part because a straight white woman from Iowa transcended the league, and too many people around the sport could not accept her success without filtering it through race, sexuality, and privilege.

Rather than treat Clark's popularity as a historic opportunity for women's basketball, they treated it as a grievance. They framed her fame as "white privilege." They called her fans "racists" for defending her.

Such dishonest framework guaranteed resentment. It also guaranteed backlash.

Rinse and repeat.

The likes of Elle Duncan have done far more to poison the conversation surrounding the WNBA than Clark or her fans have.

She did so again by describing the very people stirring the resentment as the victims.

item.title: Furious crowds protest sky-high housing costs and mass tourism in major city
item.description: Barcelona's mayor says tourist taxes still aren't high enough as Spain's mass tourism and vacation rental crisis continue to spark angry and loud protests by residents.
item.content:encoded:
Growing tensions between tourists and locals hit a boiling point in Spain recently as hundreds of thousands of residents flooded the streets of Barcelona, Madrid and other Spanish cities to protest skyrocketing housing costs.

A housing affordability crisis is at the center of the unrest, fueled in part by short-term vacation rentals, an issue Barcelona Mayor Jaume Collboni has publicly addressed.

Residents are arguing mass tourism has priced them out, with real estate companies converting apartments into lucrative vacation stays. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez addressed the issue recently at an event in Barcelona.

ANGRY LOCALS BLOCK FAMOUS BEACH AS MASS TOURISM PROTESTS ESCALATE AT VACATION HOT SPOT

"Finding an apartment in Barcelona definitely gave me a better understanding of how competitive the housing market can be," travel writer Jordi Lippe-McGraw, who moved to Barcelona from New York City six weeks ago, told Fox News Digital.

"It's a city where so many people want to live. There's a lot of pressure on available housing."

Barcelona and the surrounding region welcomed a total of 26.1 million visitors in 2025, which generated an estimated $15.4 billion in direct tourism spending, according to the Barcelona Tourism Observatory.

Frustrated locals have protested loudly and defiantly.

BRAZEN PICKPOCKETS PREY ON VULNERABLE TOURISTS AS VACATION ISLAND IS SWARMED BY MILLIONS

Amid the pressure, the federal and local governments are trying to implement change.

"Barcelona began rethinking tourism ... back in 2017," José Antonio Donaire, the commissioner for sustainable tourism, told The New York Times this summer.

"But the message of the city now is: Not one tourist more."

In September, the forced eviction of María del Carmen Abascal, an 87-year-old Spanish pensioner, became a symbol of the affordability crisis, Fox News Digital reported earlier.

After she died Oct. 7, thousands took to the streets in Madrid, Valencia, Barcelona, Hospitalet de Llobregat, Málaga and other cities.

AMERICANS EMERGE AS SOUGHT-AFTER VISITORS AS VACATION ISLAND FACES TOURISM BACKLASH

Short-term vacation rentals are part of the dispute.

On April 1, Barcelona combined a flat $5.60 (€5.00) city surcharge with the regional Catalan tourist tax, creating one of the highest visitor taxes in Europe, according to the Barcelona City Council.

That raised the total overnight tax for hotel guests to between $7.84 (€7.00) and $13.44 (€12.00) per person, per night, according to the Catalan Tax Agency.

In September 2026, Barcelona also finalized plans to restrict short-stay cruise tourism.

The Barcelona City Council initially approved raising the municipal tourist tax surcharge for short-stay cruise visitors to the legal maximum of $27 per day, according to the official city council portal.

Lippe-McGraw said the crowds are palpable in tourist areas, but the neighborhood where she lives is largely shielded from protests.

"We were aware of this sort of anti-tourist sentiment before arriving, which definitely weighed on our minds," she said. 

"Some of Barcelona's most popular areas — like the Gothic Quarter, Las Ramblas, the Sagrada Familia — can be incredibly crowded even on a random Tuesday afternoon.

"I can understand how frustrating that must be if you're a resident who's simply trying to get to work, running errands or going about your day."

Lippe-McGraw has traveled across all seven continents and said mass tourism has hit many major cities in her experience.

"How do you decide who is allowed to come and see Venice or see Barcelona versus who is not?" she asked.

Yet locals have been very welcoming to her family, she said.

"Everybody has been welcoming us, even in day-to-day interactions at the store, at the pharmacy, dealing with a plumber," she said.

"We are trying to make an effort to speak Spanish, learn the cultural norms. … And I think making an effort to understand the culture, learn the language and being respectful of local customs goes a long way." 

Brittany Miller and Ashley J. DiMella of Fox News Digital, as well as Teresa Mull, contributed reporting.

item.title: Woman found floating in sea after going overboard from Royal Caribbean ship
item.description: A 44-year-old woman clung to a lifebuoy for 20 hours in the Ionian Sea after reportedly jumping from Royal Caribbean's Odyssey of the Seas near Zakynthos.
item.content:encoded:

The 44-year-old Salvadoran national was traveling aboard Odyssey of the Seas as it sailed through the Ionian Sea near the island of Zakynthos on Saturday, the Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs told USA Today.

The cargo ship MSC Rossella III was assisting in the search and spotted the woman inside the bright orange lifebuoy in dark waters. The vessel alerted authorities, and a Greek Coast Guard crew arrived to toss her ropes and pull her to safety.

The woman reportedly told authorities she jumped off the ship because she "wanted to disembark," a Coast Guard spokesperson told Agence France-Presse, adding that "she was 20 hours at sea."

Following her rescue, she was transported to the port of Katakolo and brought to a local hospital, where a prosecutor ordered a psychiatric evaluation, according to the Hellenic Coast Guard.

CARNIVAL CRUISE SHIP PASSENGER DIES AFTER FALLING FROM BALCONY – FBI INVESTIGATES HIGH-SEAS HORROR

Fox News Digital reached out to Royal Caribbean for comment.

The incident follows a similar stunt last year when a man jumped off Royal Caribbean's Rhapsody of the Seas in San Juan, Puerto Rico, in an attempt to evade nearly $17,000 in gambling debt.
